title: How to price client work without guessing
description: Hourly billing punishes you for getting faster and invites scope creep. Here is the arithmetic behind value-based packages, and how to defend the number when a client asks where it came from.
author: Mara Vane
pullQuote: The hourly rate is a tax on getting better at your job.
content:
Hourly billing has one honest use: work whose shape nobody can predict. Everything else — the six-page site, the brand refresh, the app you have built four versions of already — is a fixed scope wearing a stopwatch, and the stopwatch is costing you money.

The problem with an hourly rate is that it prices your inexperience. The first time you built a marketing site it took ninety hours. You are now good enough to do it in thirty, and the client pays a third as much for a better result. You have been punished, precisely, for getting better at your job.

The hourly rate is a tax on getting better at your job.Every freelancer, eventually

Start from the outcome, not the calendar

Before you put a number on anything, write one sentence describing what changes for the client when the work is done. Not "a new website" — that is a deliverable. Something closer to "the spring campaign has somewhere to land, and the blog stops being a reason not to send traffic."

That sentence is your anchor. A six-page site that unblocks a campaign is not worth the same as a six-page site for a project nobody is waiting on, even though the deliverable is identical. Pricing the outcome is not a trick; it is just refusing to pretend those two projects are the same job.

Build three packages, not one number

A single number invites a negotiation, because the only two moves available are accept and haggle. Two options invite a coin flip. Three options change the question the client is asking themselves from "should I do this?" to "which of these should I do?" — which is a much better question to be arguing about.

Structure them so the middle one wins:

  • Essential — the smallest version that still solves the problem. It should be genuinely viable, not a straw man. Roughly 65% of the middle.
  • Complete — what you would actually recommend. This is the one you want them to pick, so it carries the things that make the project succeed rather than merely ship.
  • Partner — Complete plus the ongoing relationship: support, iteration, a retainer. Roughly 150% of the middle.

Most clients pick the middle. The ones who pick Partner were always going to spend that money somewhere, and the ones who pick Essential would otherwise have ghosted you entirely.

Where the middle number comes from

Work it out in this order, and write each figure down:

  1. Your floor. Realistic days, multiplied by what a day must earn for your year to work. Not what you would like to earn — what makes the maths close.
  2. The market band. What comparable work sold for near you. If a six-page build with a migration runs $8,000–$12,000 in your city, that band is a fact about the world, not an opinion about your worth.
  3. The outcome multiplier. If the project unblocks something with a date attached, it sits at the top of the band. If it is a nice-to-have with a vague timeline, the bottom.

If your floor comes out above the market band, you have found something important: either the scope is too big for the budget, or this client is not the right client. Both are worth knowing before you send anything.

Defending the number

You will be asked where it came from. The answer is never "that is my rate" — that is a shrug in a suit. The answer is the arithmetic: this many templates, this migration, these two review rounds, this support window. When a client can see the parts, "it is too expensive" turns into "can we drop the migration?" — which is a conversation about scope, and one you can win.

That is the whole trick. Price the outcome, show the parts, and give them three doors instead of one.

title: Writing a scope that still holds in week six
description: Every overrun starts as a sentence that sounded reasonable in January. The exclusions list is the most valuable page in your proposal — here is how to write one that does not read as hostile.
author: Theo Adeyemi
content:
Every overrun starts as a sentence that sounded reasonable in January. "Plus a few small tweaks to the existing pages." "We'll keep the blog roughly as-is." By March those sentences have grown teeth, and you are working weekends for free because you were being agreeable in a document.

A scope is not a description of the work. It is a boundary around the work, and boundaries are made of the things you say you will not do.

Write deliverables as countable nouns

Compare these two lines:

  • Design and build the new marketing site.
  • Six unique page templates: home, about, two service pages, a blog index, and a post template. Responsive at three breakpoints. Built in the client's existing CMS.

The first cannot be finished — there is no state of the world in which it is unambiguously done. The second can be counted, and a thing that can be counted can be delivered, invoiced, and closed.

The test: could a stranger, holding only your scope, tell you whether the project is complete? If not, the line is a feeling, not a deliverable.

The exclusions list is the most valuable page

Nobody enjoys writing it. It feels adversarial, like you are anticipating a fight before the work has started. But the exclusions list is the only part of the proposal that will still be earning its keep in week six.

It does not need to be aggressive. It needs to be specific:

Not included: content entry beyond the twelve pages listed above, third-party plugin licences, copywriting for new pages, or ongoing SEO work after launch. Any of these can be added — see the change process below.

Notice the last sentence. An exclusions list that only says no reads as defensive. One that says "not included, and here is how to include it" reads as organised, and quietly tells the client that more scope is available at a price.

Name the change process before you need it

Write one short paragraph explaining what happens when something new comes up. It should say: new work gets quoted, the quote is approved in writing, and the timeline moves accordingly. Three sentences.

The point is not the process. It is that you have both read it while everyone was still being friendly. Invoking a clause you agreed on in January is administrative; inventing one in March is a confrontation.

Assumptions are exclusions in disguise

Write down what you are assuming to be true. "The client provides all copy by the end of week two." "The existing brand assets are available as vectors." "There is one approver."

Each assumption is a small dependency you have identified in advance. When one turns out to be false — and one always does — you are pointing at a line you both read, rather than making a case from memory.

The week-six test

Before you send it, read the scope as if it is week six and the project has gone sideways. The client wants a fifth service page. The copy is three weeks late. Someone new has joined the approval chain and does not like the colour.

For each of those, ask: does the document answer this, in a line I could point at without sounding like I am improvising? If it does, send it. If it does not, you have found the paragraph you still need to write — and it will take ten minutes now, or a weekend later.

title: The follow-up that wins the job
description: Most proposals are not rejected, they are forgotten. Three emails, three timings, and the one sentence that restarts a thread everyone had given up on.
author: Priya Raman
content:
Most proposals are not rejected. They are opened on a Tuesday, read on a phone, put aside for "when I have five minutes to think properly", and then buried by everything else that landed that week. The work was never the problem. The silence was.

Following up feels like begging. It is not. Your client asked you for a document, you sent them one, and they have lost it in an inbox — reminding them is a service, provided you do it like a person.

Three emails, three jobs

Send three, spaced deliberately. Each one does a different job, and none of them says "just checking in."

Day three — make it easy to reply

The proposal is still warm. The only obstacle is that a full response feels like homework, so remove the homework: ask a question that can be answered in four words.

Hi Dana — no rush at all. Did the middle package look about right, or would it help if I put together something leaner?

"Yes" and "leaner please" are both complete answers. You have made replying cheaper than not replying.

Day eight — add something

Never send an empty nudge. Bring one new thing: a relevant piece of work, a note about timing, an observation about their site you did not include the first time.

One more thought on the migration — we did the same move for a client last year and the redirects were the whole job. I've added a line to the scope covering it so it doesn't turn into a surprise. Same number.

This is a follow-up that improves their position. It is very hard to be annoyed by.

Day fifteen — close the loop honestly

The most effective of the three, and the one people are most afraid to send. Give them a graceful exit.

Totally understand if the timing isn't right — happy to park this and pick it up later in the year. Just let me know either way and I'll stop cluttering your inbox.

Roughly a third of dead threads answer this one, and a good share of those answers are yes. The rest give you a clean no, which is worth more than a maybe you are still carrying in March.

Stop when they reply

Obvious, and yet: the fastest way to undo three good emails is a fourth that fires automatically after they have already answered. If you automate the sequence, make sure a reply cancels the rest of it.

What to do with the silence

If all three go unanswered, let it go — and write down why you think it went quiet. Wrong budget, wrong timing, wrong contact, no real project behind it. Do that for twenty proposals and a pattern shows up, and the pattern is usually about which enquiries you should be taking on at all.

That is the actual value of following up properly. Not the individual job you rescue, but the honest record of what happens after you press send.

title: Eight questions to ask before you quote
description: Ten minutes of questions, answered in writing, will tell you more about whether a job is worth doing than an hour on a call where everyone is being pleasant.
author: Jonas Meyer
content:
The cheapest project rescue in the world happens before you send a number. Ten minutes of questions, answered in writing, will tell you more about whether this job is worth doing than an hour on a call where everyone is being nice to each other.

Send these before you quote. Not after the kickoff — before the number.

The eight

1. What has to be true for this to be a success?

Open, deliberately. The answer tells you whether they are buying a website or buying a campaign that needs somewhere to land. Those are different projects at different prices.

2. Is there a date this has to be live by, and what is attached to it?

"March" is a preference. "March, because the trade show is the 14th" is a constraint with money behind it, and it changes both the schedule and the price.

3. What range were you expecting to invest?

The question everyone skips. Ask it plainly and give them a band to react to — "most projects like this land between eight and fifteen thousand; does that sound about right?" You are not being rude, you are saving you both a fortnight.

4. Who signs this off?

And the follow-up that matters more: is there anyone else whose opinion will matter in week five? Late-arriving stakeholders are the single most reliable cause of a project doubling in length.

5. What exists already?

Brand assets, copy, photography, a CMS, an analytics setup. Every "yes" here is work you do not have to price. Every "we'll sort that out later" is a risk you should be writing into your assumptions.

6. Who is providing the words?

Copy is the number one cause of a stalled build, and it is almost never in the scope. Ask directly. If the answer is "we'll write it ourselves", put a date on it in the timeline and mark it as a dependency.

7. What has been tried before, and what went wrong?

You learn two things: the practical history of the project, and how they talk about the last person who worked on it. Pay close attention to the second one.

8. How do you want to work together?

Weekly calls or async updates? Slack or email? One reviewer or a committee? This looks like a soft question and it is really a pricing question — a project with four approvers and a standing Monday call costs more to run than one with a single decision-maker.

Send it in writing

Ask these in a form or an email, not on a call. Written answers are considered answers, they can be pasted into the scope, and they can be pointed at later when someone remembers the budget differently.

The other thing that happens: a client who will not spend ten minutes answering eight questions is telling you something important about what the next three months would have been like.
